name: Lip stencil / bone structure hack: orthotropics for lip support

lead: In mewing and orthotropics circles, the idea is that holding a tongue and jaw posture can change the bone beneath the lips, giving better lip support and a more balanced profile.

Mewing is oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on pressing the tongue against the palate. Reference sources describe it as unproven, say the American Association of Orthodontists sees no evidence it improves the jaw, and do not address lips or soft-tissue profile.

paras: Practitioners rest the tongue against the palate, keep the lips sealed and breathe through the nose, as a constant background habit maintained over months or years.
Potential risks cited include jaw joint problems, bite changes and delayed orthodontic care in children.

angle.text: Mewing and orthotropics circles say tongue posture can reshape the bone under the lips to improve profile. The posture is held daily, and followers expect better lip support over time. Reference sources describe mewing as unproven and do not cover lips.

lead: This entry covers the claim, circulated in mewing and orthotropics circles, that jaw and facial posture training can change the profile of the lips by altering the bone structure that supports them. People pursue it hoping for fuller-looking, better-supported lips and a more balanced profile without cosmetic procedures. Mewing is a form of oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on resting the tongue against the roof of the mouth.[1]

Proponents reason that if the upper jaw and teeth sit further forward, the lips gain support and a different profile. Orthodontic research does show that lips follow tooth movement: in a 2020 University of Iowa study of 60 adults treated with braces, horizontal upper lip movement matched upper incisor crown movement at roughly a one-to-one ratio.[2] Those findings concern orthodontic tooth movement, not posture training.

Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven form of oral posture training, states that no credible scientific research has proven the efficacy of orthotropics, and reports that the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it improves the jaw. It does not address lips or soft tissue.[1]
infobox: Upper lip moved about 1:1 with upper incisor in one braces study [2]

paras: Orthotropics holds that oral posture guides jaw and facial growth, in contrast to conventional orthodontics, which focuses on aligning teeth. The lip-related claim extends this: if the jaws move forward or the upper jaw widens, the lips are said to gain support and a different profile. The reference articles on mewing do not describe lip outcomes.[1]

Mewing is named after British orthodontist John Mew. His son Mike Mew is also associated with it; Wikipedia reports Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and, in 2024, struck from the UK dental register after a misconduct hearing involving child patients. Mewing went viral on social media from 2019, especially within looksmaxxing subcultures.[1]

sections.h: Teeth, bone and lip position in orthodontics
paras: In conventional orthodontics, lip position changes with incisor movement. The 2020 Iowa cephalometric thesis of 30 extraction and 30 non-extraction adult cases found upper lip movement tracked the upper incisor crown at roughly 1:1, and that upper incisor angulation increased about 6.8 degrees in the non-extraction group and decreased about 4.3 degrees in the extraction group.[2] Other orthodontic work on lip response varies between individuals, according to the authors of these studies, and that research concerns braces rather than posture training.

The American Association of Orthodontists and the Cleveland Clinic are reported to state that there is no credible scientific evidence that mewing reshapes the face or jawline. Wikipedia says most orthodontists do not consider mewing a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery.[1] Potential risks cited for the practice include temporomandibular joint disorders, bite problems and delayed orthodontic care in children.

No studies found on orthotropics or mewing changing lip profile. Related work exists on orofacial myofunctional therapy: 2025 pilot studies reported effects on hyoid position and jaw pain, but they did not directly test mewing or lip outcomes. Separate orthodontic research on tooth movement and lip position is described above.[2]

lore.intro: Mewing communities discuss lip support as one possible by-product of posture training, alongside jawline and midface claims.

claims.claim: Mewing can change lip profile by moving the underlying bone structure.

timeline.event: Mewing goes viral on social media, especially in looksmaxxing communities.[1]
